titleStmt.title: Intelligence Memorandum Prepared in the Central Intelligence Agency

div.head: 385. Intelligence Memorandum Prepared in the Central Intelligence Agency
div.p: ECUADOR: The Febres-Cordero Administration After One Year

President Leon Febres-Cordero’s state visit to Washington in January comes at the one-and-a-half year point in his four-year term and at a time when he has made some significant progress on several fronts. In particular, he has made great strides in setting the country on the road to a slow but steady economic recovery by adopting market-oriented strategies to promote entrepreneurial activity, stimulate investment, and revive growth. His economic and financial moves, some of them politically difficult, are already producing positive results in both external accounts and domestic recovery. The chief threat to this economic revival is the weakness of the world market for oil, Ecuador’s chief foreign exchange earner. Febres-Cordero also has launched a vigorous and successful drug enforcement campaign, with Ecuador accounting for 25 percent of the cocaine hydrochloride seized in South America in the first half of 1985. Despite his highly publicized and divisive legislative battles—often leading to charges that he has dictatorial tendencies—the President has consolidated his power base by gaining control of Congress and is close to attaining a majority in the Supreme Court. His principal shortcomings to date—failure to control the fledgling guerrilla organization Alfaro Vive, Carajo—is largely attributable to the military’s inability and unwillingness to develop an effective counterinsurgency capability.

During his scheduled meeting with President Reagan, Febres-Cordero is likely to request substantial increases in US assistance, particularly for counterinsurgency
training, and added training and funding for drug enforcement efforts. He probably will argue that, as a strong proponent of democracy and free enterprise and because of his vigorous efforts to combat Communism, drug trafficking and terrorism, the United States should be more forthcoming with aid to what he sees as Washington’s staunchest ally in South America.
[Omitted here is the body of the paper.]

note.p: Source: Department of State, Bureau of Inter-American Affairs, Assistant Secretary Files, Special Collection—Iran Contra—Noriega, Lot 95D407, Ecuador/Uruguay. Secret; Noforn; [handling restriction not declassified]. Prepared in the South American Division, Office of African and Latin American Analysis and the Office of Central Reference and coordinated with DO. Prepared at the request of Tillman. Information available as of December 1985 was used in the preparation of the paper.

In a November 29 memorandum to Reagan, McFarlane noted “Shultz’s strong interest in upgrading the Febres-Cordero visit to a State visit,” and wrote: “We believe that President Febres-Cordero of Ecuador merits a State visit. He is one of the few Latin Americans vigorously implementing free market economic policies, has taken a strong stand against the Sandinistas, and has cooperated extensively with the U.S. on narcotics and other important issues. He is an open and enthusiastic friend of the United States. We would like to highlight this cooperation and friendship and strongly support the Department of State and Secretary Shultz’s request that his visit be upgraded from an official working visit to a State visit. The Department of State has requested expedited treatment of this request because of time constraints.” Reagan approved. (Reagan Library, NSC Records, Latin American Affairs Directorate, Country File, Ecuador (12/31/1985–03/31/1986))
